title: Two ENISA Reports, Two Different Things: Startup Certification vs the Entrepreneur Permit
excerpt: ENISA appears in two Spanish laws. Under the Startups Law it certifies companies as "emerging" for tax and corporate benefits, within three months. Under Law 14/2013 it reports on a founder's project for a residence permit, within ten working days. Founders mix them up constantly.
keyTakeaway: Startup certification under Law 28/2022 is for a company that already exists and meets seven conditions, decided in up to three months. The report for the entrepreneur permit under Law 14/2013 is about your project and profile, issued in ten working days. You do not need the first to get the second.
summaryEn: Explains the difference between ENISA's certification of an "empresa emergente" under Spain's Law 28/2022 and ENISA's report on an entrepreneur residence permit under Law 14/2013, from the two BOE texts.

faq.q: Do I need my company certified as a startup to get the entrepreneur permit?
faq.a: No. The permit's report under article 70 of Law 14/2013 assesses your profile, business plan and added value. Startup certification under article 4 of Law 28/2022 is a separate procedure for an existing company seeking the Startups Law's benefits.

Article 3 of Law 28/2022 lists seven conditions that must all be met, including being no more than five years old (seven in some sectors), never having paid dividends, not being listed, having its seat or a permanent establishment in Spain, and having 60% of staff employed in Spain.

faq.q: How long does each ENISA procedure take?
faq.a: Certification: up to three months from a complete application, with positive silence if ENISA does not answer. The permit report: ten working days from the UGE's request.

content:
A sentence we hear from founders more than any other about Spain goes roughly: "I need to get my startup certified by ENISA for the visa." It is half right, and the wrong half costs months. ENISA, Spain's Empresa Nacional de Innovación, does two different jobs under two different laws, and the one the sentence describes is not the one the permit needs. This article separates them using the texts themselves: Law 28/2022, the Startups Law, and Law 14/2013 as amended by it. Both read on 8 November 2026.

Job one: certifying a company as "emerging"

The Startups Law applies to "empresas emergentes", and article 3 defines them. A company qualifies only if it meets every one of these conditions:

  1. It is newly created, or no more than five years have passed since its incorporation deed was registered; seven years for biotechnology, energy, industrial and other strategic sectors, or for companies that developed their own technology designed entirely in Spain.
  2. It did not come out of a merger, spin-off or transformation of companies that were not themselves startups.
  3. It has never distributed dividends.
  4. It is not listed on a regulated market.
  5. Its registered office or a permanent establishment is in Spain.
  6. 60% of its workforce is on employment contracts in Spain.
  7. It runs an innovative project with a scalable business model, as article 4 defines it.

Article 4 is where ENISA comes in. A founder who wants the law's benefits asks ENISA to evaluate the company against articles 3 and 6 and for the innovative and scalable character of the model. ENISA has up to three months from a complete application; if it does not answer, the request counts as granted by positive silence, and the clock stops while documents are requested. The criteria are a list any investor would recognise: innovation, including public funding received in the last three years and R&D spend over the last two years, or one for younger firms; market attractiveness and traction; stage, from prototype to minimum viable product to market; scalability of users, operations or revenue; competition and differentiation; the team; dependence on suppliers and leases; customers. ENISA may refuse where the model raises reputational, regulatory, ethical or speculative doubts, and must publish a procedure guide.

Notice what this is about: a legal person, already incorporated, with staff, accounts and a registration date. The benefits that follow, in tax, corporate and labour law, are for that company.

Job two: reporting on a founder's project for a residence permit

Law 14/2013, article 70 as rewritten in 2022, asks a different question. An entrepreneurial activity, for the residence permit, is one that is innovative and/or of special economic interest for Spain, and the evidence is a favourable report from ENISA. The UGE requests that report itself when you file; it is mandatory, and it must be issued within ten working days. What ENISA weighs here is: your professional profile and involvement, with each partner assessed whether or not they need a visa; your business plan, describing the project, the product or service and its financing, including the investment required and the possible sources; and the elements that bring added value, innovation or investment opportunities to Spain.

Nothing in that list is a company age, a dividend history, a listing or a payroll percentage. It is a project and a person. You can be assessed before the company exists, which is exactly the position of most applicants.

Side by side

  • Legal basis. Certification: articles 3 and 4 of Law 28/2022. Permit report: article 70 of Law 14/2013.
  • Subject. Certification: an incorporated company. Permit report: a founder and a plan.
  • Test. Certification: seven conditions, all required, plus innovative and scalable. Permit report: innovative and/or of special economic interest.
  • Clock. Certification: up to three months, positive silence. Permit report: ten working days from the UGE's request; the permit decision itself has its own 20-day clock at the UGE.
  • Who asks ENISA. Certification: the founders, directly. Permit report: the UGE, ex officio, after you file.
  • What you get. Certification: access to the Startups Law's benefits. Permit report: the document the UGE needs to grant residence.

Why the confusion exists

The same agency, the same word "innovative", the same year. Law 28/2022 both created the certification and rewrote the permit's article 70 to name ENISA, so pages written in 2023 often describe the two in one breath. Add that ENISA runs one portal, and a founder reading "apply to ENISA" cannot tell which door is meant. The permit's door is opened by the UGE when you file; the certification's door you open yourself, later, with a company.

What to do

  1. For the permit, prepare what article 70 names: your profile, a plan with product, financing and sources, and the value for Spain. File with the UGE; it will ask ENISA.
  2. Do not wait for, or pay for, "startup certification" before filing. It is not a prerequisite, and you cannot hold it for a company that does not exist yet.
  3. Once you have incorporated in Spain, read article 3 against your company. If all seven conditions hold, certification under article 4 becomes a real option for the benefits it unlocks, a separate decision for a later day.

The Spain guide walks the permit file in order, and the route finder says whether Spain is the file to open.
